title: Program!
excerpt: You have been surrounded by programmed media your entire life. But it has never been this powerful, or this dangerous to ignore. Defend your mind. Build alternatives together. Program, or be programmed.
content_html:
November 02, 2026 

In the 20th century we had radio and television programs; a television executive at ABC could program Thursday nights as a comedy block; the television itself became the vessel for playing Video Computer System game programs in the 1970s. By the 1980s one could program their VCR to record television or even program their home computer on that same screen.

Programs have been ubiquitous your entire life. You heard them. You watched them. You played them. You may have even made them. And as broadcasting has given way to narrowcasting and analog signals have given way to digital software, programs are increasingly watching you and using that information to alter everything from prices to our perception of reality.

We have all noticed this but no one seems to know what to do about it. He have created a world where anyone can program media - including the programs themselves. While access has never been greater, literacy has never been lower. The vast majority of people haven’t been taught even the most basic principles of this new media. We are ignorantly grazing in a field filled with danger - unable to understand the warnings so many have been shouting for decades.

The Warnings

The arrival of programmable interactive media led to a frenzied interest that crescendoed in the 1990s with the introduction of the DVD and the world wide web. By this point, the information age had become tangible in the everyday life of ordinary people. But people generally engaged new media like they did television: passively. But programmeable media is too powerful to tolerate passive consumption. Realizing this, a group of media theorists emerged to publish the Principles of Technorealism on March 12, 1998.The twelve original contributors were David Bennahum, Brooke Shelby Biggs, Paulina Borsook, Marisa Bowe, Simson Garfinkel, Steven Johnson, Douglas Rushkoff, Andrew Shapiro, David Shenk, Steve Silberman, Mark Stahlman and Stefanie Syman. The final document was based on the concept originated by Shapiro, Shenk and Johnson. They opined that “in a world driven by the flow of information, the interfaces – and the underlying code – that make information visible are becoming enormously powerful social force, [therefore] the creation of better tools should be an important part of being an involved citizen. These tools affect our lives as much as laws do, and we should subject them to a similar democratic scrutiny.” Or as Technorealist contributor Douglas Rushkoff summed it up, program or be programmed.

Rushkoff is not a computer programmer in any formal sense. He is a media theoretician. So while he laments the absence of ubiquitous computer programming education in US public schools, he is really talking about digital media more broadly.

Digital media takes the notion of “analog programs” as we saw them on television and turns them into flexible, programmable code. Today that often means code that drives capital intensive recommendation algorithms which now underpin the media ecosystem. If not as social media, then as the innocuous Google News app that defaults on your phone. If not as the Google News app, then as the digital newspaper that is constantly re-configuring itself based on engagement metricsAs C. Thi Nguyen has said, “Metrics are technology that standardize attention.” from social media and the hundreds of advertising networks that fester in the ecosystem like flies on a decaying corpse.The Technorealists proposed to guard against this form of Surveillance Capitalism 16 years before the term was coined. Point 3 of the manifesto reads: “Government has an important role to play on the electronic frontier […] it is foolish to say that the public has no sovereignty over what an errant citizen or fraudulent corporation does online. […] Technology standards and privacy issues, for example, are too important to be entrusted to the marketplace alone. Competing software firms have little interest in preserving the open standards that are essential to a fully functioning interactive network. Markets encourage innovation, but they do not necessarily insure the public interest.”

The 225 partners of DWnoyb recently filed a GDPR complaint against dict.cc due to their consent agreement featuring an astounding 1,741 partners. ‘Felix Mikolasch, data protection lawyer at noyb: “It would take days or even weeks to properly read and understand the data protection policies of 1,741 companies. It is ridiculous to assume that this would allow for an informed decision.”’ by David Schmudde is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0  

The internet is truly a different type of media; digital interactivity facilitates the same physical reach to both the institutional power and the distributed peer. The interface to this media is a sophisticated language colloquially known as programming.The name programming elides its expressive power, which is somewhere between mathematics and natural language. And if you do not know how to speak it, the institutional powers will speak it for you.

Take the basic example of RSS/atom. I love RSS and use it to this day. The premise is simple: in a diverse information ecosystem, you can select feeds from major corporate news agencies, collectively funded information providers, and self-funded bloggers and they all get equal space in your reader. The feed is flexible; the sources inevitably change from year to year as you discover new things and get tired of old things. But this intellectual freedom comes at a cost - you must make choices. You must create the program. The alternative is an algorithmically defined news app that makes the program for you. And the organization controlling that program makes tiny, seemingly innocuous tweaks every week which can have profound consequences over time.For example, the person who added the infinite scroll to the Facebook timeline, Aza Raskin, now says he regrets it. It turns out that removing the “next page” button is a great way to keep people on Facebook but not a great way to consciously use time. Or how about the time that Amazon paid the USA Federal Trade Commission $2.5 billion to settle a case built around what its own employees called the “Iliad Flow” - an Amazon Prime-cancellation process spread across four pages and fifteen options, where every button except one routed a user back to the start. Leaked internal documents showed that when Amazon simplified the flow, cancellations dropped 14 percent, so the company reversed course and kept the maze.

Digital media’s flexibility, reach, subtlety, and power demands our active engagement unique to any other preceding media.

On Speaking

The ability to speak the language of programming tended to favor white males - but not exclusively and not historically. When programming was less well-compensated and less highly regarded, it was a job for women. And as Prophets of Computing demonstrates, there have been a large number of local approaches to machine programming throughout Asia and Latin America.

But the current crop of programmers - the people who by definition control programmed media - does seem like more of a monoculture. A more egalitarian world is possible but we will not arrive there in a generation by putting iPads in classrooms. The Technorealists have understood this for decades.Again from the Technorealists: “Wiring the schools will not save them. The problems with America’s public schools – disparate funding, social promotion, bloated class size, crumbling infrastructure, lack of standards – have almost nothing to do with technology. Consequently, no amount of technology will lead to the educational revolution prophesied by President Clinton and others. The art of teaching cannot be replicated by computers, the Net, or by ‘distance learning.’ These tools can, of course, augment an already high-quality educational experience. But to rely on them as any sort of panacea would be a costly mistake.” To the contrary, multiple studies have shown that tablets and laptops largely detract from the learning environmentThe Laptop and the Lecture: The Effects of Multitasking in Learning Environments (Hembrooke & Gay, 2003); Dividing Attention in the Classroom Reduces Exam Performance (Glass & Kang, 2019); Examining the impact of off-task multi-tasking with technology on real-time classroom learning (Wood et al., 2011); Don’t Throw Away Your Printed Books: A Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Reading Media on Reading Comprehension (Delgato et al., 2018), etc… and tablets are a poor tool for teaching programming; they are designed primarily for media consumption.

LLMs are the latest consumer layer of digital media. At a minimum, they promise to become a metamediaMarshall McLuhan coined the term “metamedia“ to describe the relationship between form and content, especially in the context of new technologies and new media. of our everyday lives. Much has been written about how LLMs will eliminate the entire field of programming - as if people will no longer need to know how to speak for themselves. Programming will still exist. But much will be obscured by a consumer veneer.

The language of programming is actually the language of systems. Self-trained hackers were aware of this language when they were hacking the telephone networks of the 1970s. And freshmen at MIT in the 1980s understood this after reading the Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs. Humans build systems. And systems contribute to our view of the world that we are born into. LLMs can provide a surface-level understanding of a system but only hands-on experience can provide knowledge.

You are constrained by any system that you cannot inspect. This is true of both designed and emergent systems such as cities, forests, and networks. The natural sciences, including informatics,The term informatics is often used interchangeably with computer science - where the latter focuses on either the theory of computation or the study of the physical computer. produces the notation we use to describe what we know about these systems. As long as there are systems and networks, there will be programming.

On Mind

The physical computer is unique because it is the artificial embodiment of a natural science. The theoretical computer has no politics. But the physical computer is bound to the systems used to create it.The first point from the Technorealist manifesto: “Technologies are not neutral. A great misconception of our time is the idea that technologies are completely free of bias – that because they are inanimate artifacts, they don’t promote certain kinds of behaviors over others. In truth, technologies come loaded with both intended and unintended social, political, and economic leanings. Every tool provides its users with a particular manner of seeing the world and specific ways of interacting with others. It is important for each of us to consider the biases of various technologies and to seek out those that reflect our values and aspirations.” And those systems have historically been large, well-funded bureaucratic projects or globally scaled, highly-capitalized consumer products. So the end result of decades of effort to “democratize computing” has produced an oligarchic class of unimaginable wealth and a consistent decade-over-decade decline in the share of any productivity gains created by the computer.“The labor share — the percentage of economic output that accrues to workers as compensation in exchange for their labor — has been declining in the nonfarm business sector throughout most of the post-World War Two era […] reaching a low of 56.0 percent in the fourth quarter of 2011.” ~ Labor share of output has declined since 1947 March 07, 2017 Or take the example of newspapers. The papers were revolutionized by productivity gains starting with the arrival of digital layout tools. The industry employed 458,000 people in June 1990 and declined to 367,200 in December 2005 while the revenues rose, profits remained strong, and the papers were a prized acquisition asset. Average employee pay did not benefit from the gains in efficiency. See also the wage calculator to see how your work has been systematically devalued since 1979.

So how do we fight back against these overwhelming odds? We program. Not as an offense into their territory. But as a defense of our territory - our mind.

Civilization is built on media. You cannot shelter your sons and daughters; you have already seen the impact on your friends and neighbors. It is past time to accept that in a programmable world of digital media, we can no longer blame the television executive or the media baron for their programs. We must support and participate in alternative systems. From food to computing - we must create and participate in systems that minimize cruelty as a bulwark against systems that maximize profit.

The lingua franca of these systems is software. This language is at least as important as the language you speak with your friends. Learning the language of systems - a.k.a programming - will be a mind-opening second or third language that you can use to manifest the world you want to see in everyday media.

Timeline

Events from this post have been added to a timeline of significant events in the history of information.

Principles of Technorealism

“Technorealism demands that we think critically about the role that tools and interfaces play in human evolution and everyday life. Integral to this perspective is our understanding that the current tide of technological transformation, while important and powerful, is actually a continuation of waves of change that have taken place throughout history. Looking, for example, at the history of the automobile, television, or the telephone -- not just the devices but the institutions they became -- we see profound benefits as well as substantial costs.” †

Haunted House for the Atari 2600

Haunted House (1982, Atari Inc.) is one of the earliest examples of the survival horror genre, which would not be well defined until Alone in the Dark (1992, Atari SA, née Infogrames) and Alien vs. Predator (1994, Atari Corp.). The scrolling playfield was innovative for its time and provided a sense that something could be lurking around the corner.

content_html_zh:
November 02, 2026

In the 20th century we had radio and television programs; a television executive at ABC could program Thursday nights as a comedy block; the television itself became the vessel for playing Video Computer System game programs in the 1970s. By the 1980s one could program their VCR to record television or even program their home computer on that same screen.

Programs have been ubiquitous your entire life. You heard them. You watched them. You played them. You may have even made them. And as broadcasting has given way to narrowcasting and analog signals have given way to digital software, programs are increasingly watching you and using that information to alter everything from prices to our perception of reality.

We have all noticed this but no one seems to know what to do about it. He have created a world where anyone can program media - including the programs themselves. While access has never been greater, literacy has never been lower. The vast majority of people haven’t been taught even the most basic principles of this new media. We are ignorantly grazing in a field filled with danger - unable to understand the warnings so many have been shouting for decades.

The Warnings

The arrival of programmable interactive media led to a frenzied interest that crescendoed in the 1990s with the introduction of the DVD and the world wide web. By this point, the information age had become tangible in the everyday life of ordinary people. But people generally engaged new media like they did television: passively. But programmeable media is too powerful to tolerate passive consumption. Realizing this, a group of media theorists emerged to publish the Principles of Technorealism on March 12, 1998.The twelve original contributors were David Bennahum, Brooke Shelby Biggs, Paulina Borsook, Marisa Bowe, Simson Garfinkel, Steven Johnson, Douglas Rushkoff, Andrew Shapiro, David Shenk, Steve Silberman, Mark Stahlman and Stefanie Syman. The final document was based on the concept originated by Shapiro, Shenk and Johnson. They opined that “in a world driven by the flow of information, the interfaces – and the underlying code – that make information visible are becoming enormously powerful social force, [therefore] the creation of better tools should be an important part of being an involved citizen. These tools affect our lives as much as laws do, and we should subject them to a similar democratic scrutiny.” Or as Technorealist contributor Douglas Rushkoff summed it up, program or be programmed.

Rushkoff is not a computer programmer in any formal sense. He is a media theoretician. So while he laments the absence of ubiquitous computer programming education in US public schools, he is really talking about digital media more broadly.

Digital media takes the notion of “analog programs” as we saw them on television and turns them into flexible, programmable code. Today that often means code that drives capital intensive recommendation algorithms which now underpin the media ecosystem. If not as social media, then as the innocuous Google News app that defaults on your phone. If not as the Google News app, then as the digital newspaper that is constantly re-configuring itself based on engagement metricsAs C. Thi Nguyen has said, “Metrics are technology that standardize attention.” from social media and the hundreds of advertising networks that fester in the ecosystem like flies on a decaying corpse.The Technorealists proposed to guard against this form of Surveillance Capitalism 16 years before the term was coined. Point 3 of the manifesto reads: “Government has an important role to play on the electronic frontier […] it is foolish to say that the public has no sovereignty over what an errant citizen or fraudulent corporation does online. […] Technology standards and privacy issues, for example, are too important to be entrusted to the marketplace alone. Competing software firms have little interest in preserving the open standards that are essential to a fully functioning interactive network. Markets encourage innovation, but they do not necessarily insure the public interest.”

The 225 partners of DWnoyb recently filed a GDPR complaint against dict.cc due to their consent agreement featuring an astounding 1,741 partners. ‘Felix Mikolasch, data protection lawyer at noyb: “It would take days or even weeks to properly read and understand the data protection policies of 1,741 companies. It is ridiculous to assume that this would allow for an informed decision.”’ by David Schmudde is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0

The internet is truly a different type of media; digital interactivity facilitates the same physical reach to both the institutional power and the distributed peer. The interface to this media is a sophisticated language colloquially known as programming.The name programming elides its expressive power, which is somewhere between mathematics and natural language. And if you do not know how to speak it, the institutional powers will speak it for you.

Take the basic example of RSS/atom. I love RSS and use it to this day. The premise is simple: in a diverse information ecosystem, you can select feeds from major corporate news agencies, collectively funded information providers, and self-funded bloggers and they all get equal space in your reader. The feed is flexible; the sources inevitably change from year to year as you discover new things and get tired of old things. But this intellectual freedom comes at a cost - you must make choices. You must create the program. The alternative is an algorithmically defined news app that makes the program for you. And the organization controlling that program makes tiny, seemingly innocuous tweaks every week which can have profound consequences over time.For example, the person who added the infinite scroll to the Facebook timeline, Aza Raskin, now says he regrets it. It turns out that removing the “next page” button is a great way to keep people on Facebook but not a great way to consciously use time. Or how about the time that Amazon paid the USA Federal Trade Commission $2.5 billion to settle a case built around what its own employees called the “Iliad Flow” - an Amazon Prime-cancellation process spread across four pages and fifteen options, where every button except one routed a user back to the start. Leaked internal documents showed that when Amazon simplified the flow, cancellations dropped 14 percent, so the company reversed course and kept the maze.

Digital media’s flexibility, reach, subtlety, and power demands our active engagement unique to any other preceding media.

On Speaking

The ability to speak the language of programming tended to favor white males - but not exclusively and not historically. When programming was less well-compensated and less highly regarded, it was a job for women. And as Prophets of Computing demonstrates, there have been a large number of local approaches to machine programming throughout Asia and Latin America.

But the current crop of programmers - the people who by definition control programmed media - does seem like more of a monoculture. A more egalitarian world is possible but we will not arrive there in a generation by putting iPads in classrooms. The Technorealists have understood this for decades.Again from the Technorealists: “Wiring the schools will not save them. The problems with America’s public schools – disparate funding, social promotion, bloated class size, crumbling infrastructure, lack of standards – have almost nothing to do with technology. Consequently, no amount of technology will lead to the educational revolution prophesied by President Clinton and others. The art of teaching cannot be replicated by computers, the Net, or by ‘distance learning.’ These tools can, of course, augment an already high-quality educational experience. Every tool provides its users with a particular manner of seeing the world and specific ways of interacting with others. It is important for each of us to consider the biases of various technologies and to seek out those that reflect our values and aspirations.” And those systems have historically been large, well-funded bureaucratic projects or globally scaled, highly-capitalized consumer products. So the end result of decades of effort to “democratize computing” has produced an oligarchic class of unimaginable wealth and a consistent decade-over-decade decline in the share of any productivity gains created by the computer.“The labor share — the percentage of economic output that accrues to workers as compensation in exchange for their labor — has been declining in the nonfarm business sector throughout most of the post-World War Two era […] reaching a low of 56.0 percent in the fourth quarter of 2011.” ~ Labor share of output has declined since 1947 March 07, 2017 Or take the example of newspapers. The papers were revolutionized by productivity gains starting with the arrival of digital layout tools. The industry employed 458,000 people in June 1990 and declined to 367,200 in December 2005 while the revenues rose, profits remained strong, and the papers were a prized acquisition asset. So how do we fight back against these overwhelming odds? We program. Not as an offense into their territory. But as a defense of our territory - our mind.

Civilization is built on media. You cannot shelter your sons and daughters; you have already seen the impact on your friends and neighbors. It is past time to accept that in a programmable world of digital media, we can no longer blame the television executive or the media baron for their programs. We must support and participate in alternative systems. From food to computing - we must create and participate in systems that minimize cruelty as a bulwark against systems that maximize profit.

The lingua franca of these systems is software. This language is at least as important as the language you speak with your friends. Learning the language of systems - a.k.a programming - will be a mind-opening second or third language that you can use to manifest the world you want to see in everyday media.

Principles of Technorealism

“Technorealism demands that we think critically about the role that tools and interfaces play in human evolution and everyday life. Integral to this perspective is our understanding that the current tide of technological transformation, while important and powerful, is actually a continuation of waves of change that have taken place throughout history. Haunted House for the Atari 2600

Haunted House (1982, Atari Inc.) is one of the earliest examples of the survival horror genre, which would not be well defined until Alone in the Dark (1992, Atari SA, née Infogrames) and Alien vs. Predator (1994, Atari Corp.). The scrolling playfield was innovative for its time and provided a sense that something could be lurking around the corner.
